subject: chem
title: Electrochemistry
subtitle: Redox, electrode potentials, electrolysis and fuel cells.
concept: Redox reactions involve simultaneous oxidation (loss of electrons) and reduction (gain of electrons); OIL RIG is the mnemonic.
Standard electrode potentials (E°) are measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE); a more positive E° means a better oxidising agent.
Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous redox reactions; products depend on ion concentration and electrode material.

notes.heading: Oxidation States and Redox
items: Oxidation state rules: O is usually −2; H is usually +1; F is always −1; sum of oxidation states = overall charge of the species. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain.

Oxidising agent: accepts electrons (is itself reduced). Reducing agent: donates electrons (is itself oxidised). To balance redox equations, write separate half-equations — balance atoms (using H₂O and H⁺), then balance charge with electrons; then combine.

notes.heading: Electrode Potentials and Cell EMF
items: Standard electrode potential (E⊖) is the EMF of a half-cell measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, E⊖ = 0.00 V) under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa, all solutions 1 mol dm⁻³).
More positive E⊖ → stronger oxidising agent (more easily reduced). More negative E⊖ → stronger reducing agent (more easily oxidised).
Cell EMF = E⊖(cathode, reduction) − E⊖(anode, oxidation). If EMF > 0, the cell reaction is feasible under standard conditions. EMF < 0 means non-spontaneous (the reverse reaction is spontaneous).

notes.heading: Electrolysis
items: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction. Cathode (negative electrode): reduction (cations are discharged). Anode (positive electrode): oxidation (anions are discharged).

Competing discharges in aqueous solution: at the cathode, H₂ is evolved from water unless the metal cation is below hydrogen in the electrochemical series (Cu²⁺, Ag⁺). At the anode, in concentrated halide solution, the halide is discharged; in dilute solution, O₂ is evolved from water (OH⁻ oxidised).

Electrolysis of molten NaCl: cathode → Na; anode → Cl₂. Purification of copper: impure Cu anode dissolves; pure Cu deposits at the cathode (other metals do not deposit if their E⊖ is very negative or very positive).

notes.heading: Fuel Cells
items: Hydrogen fuel cell: H₂ is oxidised at the anode (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻); O₂ is reduced at the cathode (O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O). Overall: H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O. Higher efficiency than combustion engines. Only H₂O produced — clean at point of use.
Disadvantages: H₂ storage (high pressure or cryogenic); currently most H₂ is made from fossil fuels (steam reforming); expensive Pt catalysts required.

definitions.body: The EMF of a half-cell measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa, 1 mol dm⁻³).
A species that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced (gains electrons).
The decomposition of a substance using electrical energy; reduction occurs at the cathode, oxidation at the anode.

workedExamples.q: Given E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, calculate the EMF of the cell and identify the spontaneous reaction.

steps.text: More positive E° = cathode (reduction): Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V). Zn/Zn²⁺ is the anode (oxidation).
Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). EMF > 0 → spontaneous.

mistakes: Confusing cathode (reduction, +terminal in electrolysis but − in cells) with anode — remember: cathode = reduction always.
Subtracting electrode potentials incorrectly — EMF = E°(cathode) − E°(anode).
Forgetting that feasibility from E° applies only under standard conditions; non-standard conditions can alter feasibility.
tips: To balance half-equations: balance atoms first (use H₂O for O, H⁺ for H), then add electrons to balance charge.
In electrolysis of aqueous solutions: concentrated → ions discharged; dilute → water products (H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode).
Fuel cell: H₂ fuel at anode (oxidised); O₂ at cathode (reduced); product is water.

flashcards.a: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons); Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

flashcards.q: What are standard conditions for electrode potential measurements?
flashcards.a: 298 K, 100 kPa, all solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³.

flashcards.q: Calculate the EMF if E°(cathode) = +0.54 V and E°(anode) = −0.44 V.
In electrolysis, what happens at the cathode?
flashcards.a: Reduction — cations are discharged (gain electrons). E.g. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

flashcards.q: What are the products at the cathode and anode during electrolysis of concentrated NaCl(aq)?
flashcards.a: Cathode: H₂ (from water). Anode: Cl₂ (chloride ions discharged at high concentration).

flashcards.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells.
flashcards.a: Advantage: only H₂O produced (clean). Disadvantage: H₂ storage is difficult; often made from fossil fuels; Pt catalyst is expensive.

questions.q: Which species is the stronger oxidising agent: E°(X) = +1.36 V or E°(Y) = +0.77 V?
questions.exp: More positive E° = species is more easily reduced = stronger oxidising agent. X (+1.36 V) is stronger.

questions.q: What is the EMF of a cell with E°(cathode) = +0.34 V and E°(anode) = −0.13 V?
In electrolysis of molten NaCl, what forms at the cathode?
questions.exp: In molten NaCl (no water), Na⁺ is reduced at the cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.

questions.q: What is oxidised in a hydrogen fuel cell?
questions.exp: H₂ is oxidised at the anode: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; O₂ is reduced at the cathode.

questions.q: A half-equation for reduction has E° = +0.80 V. What does this mean?
opts: Species is a poor oxidising agent
Species is easily reduced — good oxidising agent
questions.exp: Positive E° means the half-reaction tends to proceed as written (reduction) — the species readily accepts electrons = good oxidising agent.
